answer.answer:
Adopting a robotic process is not only a technology purchase: robotic assembly is recorded as depending on the delivery model, business model and work culture, and that dependency runs one way only, so the contract and organisational form have to move first. In practice three changes carry the weight: bring the party that will actually fabricate and assemble into the design phase early, couple the parties more tightly than a conventional split contract does (in the limit, a single firm doing design and production), and commit to prefabrication and material unification upstream of the robot. Alongside that, plan for workforce skills and, where people work beside the machine, for compliance with robot safety standards. Watch that these are preconditions rather than benefits: nothing in the evidence lets a robot deployment fix a delivery model that was left unchanged.

**The delivery model is a precondition, not an outcome**

Robotic assembly (PR4) depends on the delivery model, business model and work culture (RI12), on the finding that robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [1], peer-reviewed evidence. RI12 carries exactly 2 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges [2]: the second is AT8 dependsOn RI12, that adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models [2]. Both edges point into RI12 and none out of it, so on this record the delivery model conditions adoption and is never itself produced by it. RI12 is activated in 16 of the 50 coded cases. [2]

**What specifically changes**

- *Procurement timing.* Early contractor involvement (CO11) enables prefabrication (PR2): integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party, manufacturer, fabricator or contractor, to be involved in the early design phase, and a project delivery method that involves participants in early design should be selected [2], peer-reviewed. CO11 carries 0 inbound and 3 outbound edges, the other two being CO11 enabling offsite interior DfMA processes (PR9) [2] and CO11 enabling integrated design-DFAB processes (AT12), where BIM and early contractor involvement improve design management and increase adoption [2]. CO11 is activated in 14 of the 50 coded cases. [2]
- *Organisational coupling.* AT12 hasPrecondition CO10: technically interdependent systems require tighter organisational coupling such as a single firm, the mirroring argument [2], with vertical integration also named among management approaches for digital fabrication adoption, though that source is self-declared correlational [2]. Actor-side, interdisciplinary team integration (AC4) enables the same integrated design-DFAB process [2].
- *Product definition upstream.* PR4 hasPrecondition PR2: automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [2], and Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components (AT7 enables PR4) [2]. Where takt is short, production requires a highly detailed definition of tasks to avoid ambiguousness (PR18 hasPrecondition AR14) [2]; AR14 is activated in 28 of the 50 coded cases [2].
- *Skills and safety.* AR9 dependsOn RI6: high sophistication of digital technologies prohibits adoption by less technologically familiar workers, so skills and training are required [2], and for human-robot collaboration CO6 dependsOn RI6 (a skilled workforce) [2] and CO6 dependsOn RI18, compliance with robot safety standards, on ISO 10218-1:2025 and ISO 10218-2:2025 [2], standard-grade evidence; power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits mitigates contact-injury risk (RI20) [2]. This is what the retrieved edges establish; it is not a complete list of applicable codes or certifications.

**What the deployed record shows**

The clearest deployed instance here is process RP22, adopted to address cost and market, performing 3d printing, assembly and material handling across sitework and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, run as a mobile robot both off-site and on site, at technology readiness level 8 to 9 [3]. It activates precisely the organisational enablers named above: RP22 activates CO10, CO11, AT12, AT8, AR9 and CO12 [4], so early involvement, vertical integration, the integrated design-DFAB process and the adapted business model appear together in one delivered process rather than only in the literature. The context gives no firm for RP22, only its census record census_RXT49-1. Among the census records, census_RXH4-1 addressed cost and labor performing assembly and concrete work on the structural core and envelope at readiness level 9 [5], with Firm_166 as manufacturer [4]; census_RXH7-1 covers assembly and steelwork for cost, labor and integration at readiness level 9 [6], with no firm given. census_RXI5-1, developed by Firm_081, addressed digital, safety and integration goals in digging, heavy lift and material handling on sitework [7]. None of these records carries an explicit statement of contract form, so the delivery-model requirement rests on the dependency evidence above plus RP22's activation pattern, not on a documented contract in the case files.

**Reading the correlations**

The co-occurrence list is statistical only: AR9 co-occurs with RE6 in 44 cases, with VA2 in 43 and with RI6 in 38 [2], which tells you skills concerns travel with digital fabrication processes but does not assert direction; the directional claim there is the dependsOn edge to RI6. Note also that 1899 co-occurrence edges touch these enablers and only the 15 strongest are shown [2], so absence from that list means nothing.
